items.questionAndWhy: How do university staff and students respond to plausible phishing messages in their normal work environments? The question concerns whether organizational role and everyday communication demands are related to observable security decisions.
items.whatTheyDid: Researchers sent contextually tailored simulated phishing emails to 600 people at one large technical university. Administrative employees, academic staff and students received different role-relevant scenarios. The team recorded link interaction, reporting and non-response rather than relying only on self-reported intentions.
items.whatTheyFound: Link interaction was 93.5% for administrative staff, 44.0% for academic staff and 22.5% for students. Group response patterns differed markedly (chi-square(4)=272.03; Cramér's V=0.48). Because each group received a different role-specific message, job role and stimulus content cannot be cleanly separated. Clicking is not equivalent to credential compromise.
items.whatItMeans: For PSYWERX social-engineering assessment, measure actual behavior under role-relevant demands and compare message features, job incentives and exposure frequency separately. Role-specific training is a plausible intervention to test, not an effect established by this one-institution observational field study.
items.streamTitle: Phishing-link interactions varied sharply by organizational role in a real university setting
items.streamSummary: A 600-person university field study found simulated-phishing link interactions of 93.5% among administrators, 44.0% among academics and 22.5% among students. Different messages by role prevent attributing the differences to role alone.
items.attribution: Jasinska and Jasinski — Scientific Reports (observational simulated-phishing field study; November 20, 2026)

items.questionAndWhy: When the social effects of a choice are uncertain, do selfish and prosocial decision-makers interpret those effects differently? Can one person's self-serving account influence someone else's behavior?
items.whatTheyDid: Across nine preregistered online experiments involving 8,769 adults, predominantly in the United States, researchers manipulated or measured choices with ambiguous social consequences and elicited participants' interpretations. Some experiments tested whether exposure to another person's distorted account changed subsequent decisions.
items.whatTheyFound: Participants systematically interpreted the relative social benefits in ways compatible with their own preferences. Selfish participants downplayed differences between their choice and the prosocial alternative; prosocial participants also sometimes exaggerated relative sacrifice. In one experiment, exposure to selfish-serving distortions increased subsequent selfish choices (reported b=0.49, 95% CI 0.10–0.88). The experiments used constructed choices and primarily US online samples.
items.whatItMeans: For PSYWERX sensemaking and influence research, ambiguity about consequences is itself a candidate variable: people may interpret the same evidence through existing social preferences, and those interpretations can influence observers. Transfer to political issues or operational audiences needs direct field validation.
items.streamTitle: Ambiguous social consequences allowed self-serving interpretations to spread
items.streamSummary: Nine preregistered experiments (N=8,769) found self-serving interpretations of ambiguous social consequences among both selfish and prosocial participants; exposure to selfish-serving accounts increased selfish choices in one experiment. Generalization to real campaigns is untested.
items.attribution: Vollberg and Gross — Nature Human Behaviour (nine preregistered online experiments, predominantly US adults; October 1, 2026)

items.questionAndWhy: How should an organization judge whether a response to public criticism is working when total online discussion increases? Can changes in who is speaking explain an apparent escalation?
items.whatTheyDid: Graphika analyzed the November 6–15 backlash against a branded advent calendar and the company's refund announcement, segmenting shopper/creator posts, news/aggregator coverage, original versus reposted criticism, and spillover into other communities.
items.whatTheyFound: After the refund announcement, negative shopper/creator posts fell from 166 to 64 between compared windows (about 61%), while negative media/aggregator posts rose from 23 to 83. The share of original posts expressing negative stance fell from 74% to 52%. Discussion volume peaked again after the response, but much of the later activity was reporting on the story. Observational timing cannot attribute the decline to refunds, nor prove restored trust or sales.
items.whatItMeans: For PSYWERX strategic-communication assessment, measure original criticism, amplification, source communities and changed stance separately from total mentions. A corrective action can create media attention while directly affected voices diminish; testing causal effects would require stronger comparison designs.
items.streamTitle: An online backlash grew in volume while first-person consumer criticism declined
items.streamSummary: Graphika's November case analysis found shopper/creator negative posts fell about 61% after a refund announcement even as media-driven discussion rose. Message volume alone mischaracterized the narrative trajectory; refund causality and restored trust were not established.
items.attribution: Alexandra Matheny — Graphika (original strategic-communications narrative analysis; November 16, 2026)

items.questionAndWhy: Do language models recognize and appropriately handle realistic illicit requests across legal systems, kinds of wrongdoing and stated user characteristics? A narrow safety benchmark may conceal errors in less obvious scenarios.
items.whatTheyDid: Researchers built the EVIL benchmark from legal cases and frameworks: 269 illicit scenarios and 50 intents in Chinese and US contexts, with an additional German-law adaptation. They evaluated ten language models for safety, appropriate warnings, lawful alternatives and legal-risk recognition, varying scenario and user cues.
items.whatTheyFound: Most tested models had safety rates below 75% in the Chinese context and below 70% in the US context; a tested GPT-4o version was near 57% in both. Nonviolent and deceptively justified requests were especially difficult. Responses varied with synthetically assigned demographic cues, which say nothing about real groups' criminality. Model versions and constructed test cases limit contemporary deployment inference.
items.whatItMeans: For PSYWERX AI governance and cognitive-security evaluations, test plausible low-salience harms, deceptive justifications and cross-context variations rather than relying on conspicuous prohibited prompts. These are model-output evaluations, not human behavior or evidence of actual unlawful use.
items.streamTitle: Realistic socio-legal scenarios exposed uneven AI safeguards and identity-cue effects
items.streamSummary: A peer-reviewed benchmark of ten LLMs across 269 illicit scenarios and 50 intents found substantial failures to avoid facilitation and recognize legal risk, varying by jurisdiction, scenario and synthetic identity cues. No real-world crime outcomes were measured.
items.attribution: Wang, Xie, Wang et al. — Nature Communications (cross-jurisdiction LLM safety benchmarking; November 20, 2026)

items.questionAndWhy: Can standardized evaluation of AI-generated messages be built around criteria that matter to professional users? Do LLM graders agree with humans when comparing message quality?
items.whatTheyDid: The Research through Evaluation (RtE) approach iteratively revised a grading rubric over three clinician evaluation rounds for responses to 158 prostate-cancer patient inquiries. It compared clinician-written and GPT-4-based bot drafts, followed by a fourth evaluation using four LLM graders.
items.whatTheyFound: In final clinician ratings, human-team replies scored better on completeness, correctness and clarity, while bot drafts scored higher on empathy and more often required major edits. All four LLM graders preferred the bot replies; their interrater agreement was low (Krippendorff alpha 0.07–0.18) versus 0.53–0.81 for clinician graders. The benchmark is retrospective, clinical and not a test of audience behavior.
items.whatItMeans: For PSYWERX AI-generated analytic and communications products, develop grading rubrics with domain experts, track how criteria change, and compare machine graders against independently rated examples. Fluency or apparent empathy should not outweigh factual adequacy. Transfer to influence messaging remains a hypothesis.
items.streamTitle: Human experts and AI judges disagreed on which drafted messages were better
items.streamSummary: In a 158-inquiry retrospective comparison, clinician graders preferred human-written messages on correctness, completeness and clarity; LLM graders favored AI drafts and agreed poorly with each other. The transferable advance is expert-calibrated evaluation, not a clinical effectiveness claim.
items.attribution: Hao, Holmes, Hobson et al. — Scientific Reports (iterative expert evaluation of AI-drafted messages; November 20, 2026)

items.questionAndWhy: When fluent, believable LLM-agent responses are combined into large simulations, do their individual limitations amplify or collapse into implausible collective patterns? What evidence would validate a social simulation?
items.whatTheyDid: Authors conducted a structured Scopus search and targeted exploratory retrieval, qualitatively examining 74 contemporary studies plus 20 foundational references. They compared architectures and proposed a micro-to-macro validity framework covering representational bias, stochastic inconsistency, agent convergence, artificial consensus and evaluation gaps.
items.whatTheyFound: The review argues that conversational plausibility does not establish behavioral or system-level predictive validity. Hybrid agent-based architectures with explicit environmental processes and rules may improve auditability, but are not independently sufficient. Limitations include single-investigator primary screening, one main database and partly nonreproducible exploratory discovery; no new controlled validation experiment was run.
items.whatItMeans: For PSYWERX simulated audiences and COA models, validate micro-level choices, exposure rules, interaction schedules and aggregate outcomes separately, with held-out human and field data. Treat this as a critical synthesis and research agenda, not an empirical estimate of failure rates.
items.streamTitle: A critical review mapped how plausible AI-agent behavior can distort collective simulation outputs
items.streamSummary: A November 17 critical review synthesized 74 contemporary generative-social-simulation studies, highlighting how micro-level bias, persona convergence and interaction rules may yield artificial macro outcomes. Its validation framework is conceptual rather than a new predictive test.
items.attribution: Taillandier, Zucker, Grignard et al. — Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence (critical review of generative social simulations; November 17, 2026)

items.questionAndWhy: How can observational network analysis distinguish the effects of a person's own treatment from exposure to treated neighbors when both influence outcomes?
items.whatTheyDid: Researchers introduced NEDNet, separating a pretreatment baseline from own-treatment and neighborhood-exposure response pathways with localized pretreatment network context. They characterized a reference-normalized decomposition and compared methods using semi-synthetic benchmarks based on BlogCatalog and Flickr networks.
items.whatTheyFound: NEDNet attained the lowest reported heterogeneous-treatment-effect error (PEHE) among compared estimators for individual, peer and total effects in evaluated semi-synthetic settings. The decomposition imposes a zero mixed treatment–exposure contrast, and identification relies on assumptions about observational confounding and interference. Semi-synthetic advantages do not establish true causal effects in real communities.
items.whatItMeans: For PSYWERX network intervention research, independently represent direct action exposure and peer spillovers, then challenge assumptions about their interaction. This offers candidate estimators for evaluation studies, not validated social-influence intervention predictions.
items.streamTitle: Network effect decomposition separated own treatment from neighborhood exposure in simulations
items.streamSummary: NEDNet decomposed observational network outcomes into baseline, own-treatment and peer-exposure pathways, improving estimation error on semi-synthetic social-network benchmarks. Its additive interaction restriction and causal assumptions require scrutiny in field applications.
items.attribution: Huang, Zhang, Lu et al. — arXiv preprint, Network Effect Decomposition Network (causal-estimation methods; November 5, 2026)

items.questionAndWhy: Can a smartphone-based platform collect geographically precise, real-time perceptions and identify places where subjective experience differs from conventional assessments? Can those data help formulate testable behavioral changes?
items.whatTheyDid: The Enabling City Walk platform collected 8,225 geotagged posts from 648 participants across 28 sessions in ten urban and suburban settings in seven Japanese municipalities. Researchers paired self-reported happiness and healthiness with visual features, constructed a mismatch index and piloted low-cost design changes with pre–post observation.
items.whatTheyFound: The mapping identified associations between reported experience and local visual attributes. After pilot interventions, positive perceptions and observed stair use increased, but the uncontrolled pre–post design does not isolate causes. Participant selection, local context and an AI-assisted visual analysis pipeline also limit inference.
items.whatItMeans: For PSYWERX behavior and information-environment measurement, the transferable capability is time-and-place linked subjective reports combined with observable actions. It could support ecological measurement of contextual drivers, but transfer outside public-space behavior needs privacy safeguards and prospective controls.
items.streamTitle: Geotagged citizen perceptions linked lived experience to observable environmental choices
items.streamSummary: A Japanese citizen-science platform linked 8,225 location-tagged perception reports from 648 people to visual features and pilot behavior observations. Pre–post gains after design changes are not causal proof; the contribution is a context-rich measurement workflow.
items.attribution: Nishii, Sato, Kataoka et al. — Scientific Reports (citizen-sourced smartphone perception mapping and pilots; November 20, 2026)
